title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Welcome to the Dust Heaps

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, loving, and occasionally astonished reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be working through a book that is, by almost any measure, Dickens at the height of his powers.
Our Mutual Friend: a novel about money, death, identity, and the extraordinary uses to which a heap of dust can be put.
Three remarkable guests have joined me for this opening episode, and I want to introduce them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels for the ear than almost anyone alive — he reads Dickens the way Dickens intended, as performance, as timing, as pure theatrical delight.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows what Victorian poverty actually looked like from the inside of its institutions — and he is not sentimental about it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read this novel more times than she will readily admit, and who has strong opinions — which she will not be keeping to herself.
Welcome, all three of you.
Delighted to be here — and I should say at once that Our Mutual Friend is the Dickens novel I return to most.
It has a darkness to it that the earlier books don't quite reach.
But it is also — and this matters enormously — enormously funny.
The comic writing is some of the finest he ever produced.
Take the parade of beggars writing to Boffin after he comes into his fortune.
Dickens describes their letters — their so-called documents — and he says,
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf.
That comparison is so precise, so devastating, and so absolutely delighted with itself.
That is Dickens at full stretch.
What strikes me about that passage is the layering of it.
It's comic, yes — but there's something genuinely bleak underneath.
These are desperate people, dressed up in satirical costume.
The daughters of general officers — long accustomed to every luxury of life, Dickens says, except spelling.
That parenthetical — except spelling — is the kind of thing you re-read three times just for the pleasure of it.
But then you think: these women are actually destitute.
The joke and the tragedy occupy exactly the same space.
Caroline is right that the satire has a real bite to it — and the historical record bears that out.
When a windfall of any kind became publicly known in Victorian England, the letters would arrive within days.
The category Dickens calls the beggars of punctual business-habits — those who announce they will be cold in death at a quarter to one on Tuesday — is not pure invention.
Threatening suicide in correspondence was a documented strategy of last resort.
What Dickens understood — and this novel understands it better than almost any other — is that money creates a gravitational field.
And those in its orbit will find any language, any posture, any fiction, to pull themselves closer.
That's what Boffin's fortune unleashes — not generosity, but gravity.
Gravity — that's the word, isn't it.
And the novel sets this up from the very beginning — the Boffin fortune originates in literal dust heaps.
The will itself — when we finally get a glimpse of it through Wegg — is a masterpiece of misanthropic economy.
Wegg reads it out with such relish, and the terms of it are extraordinary.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
Which is quite enough for him.
The contempt in that phrase is magnificent — and it sets the whole novel's tone.
There's something almost wicked in how Dickens handles the Milveys in this same moral territory.
The Reverend Frank and Margaretta are genuinely good people — Dickens is clear about that, and it matters.
But then there is Mrs Sprodgkin, who haunts their doorstep with the instinct of a natural predator.
And Dickens describes her view of the bread and butter and tea she extracts from them with this extraordinary phrase.
"She regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey."
She has elevated her own imposition into a form of scripture.
That is both very funny and, if you sit with it, quite disturbing.
The Milveys are one of the novel's most quietly radical elements.
Dickens describes them as representatives of hundreds of other good Christian pairs, as conscientious and as useful.
That's a direct rebuke to those who caricatured Victorian clergy as either hypocrites or bloated sinecurists.
The actual working clergy of the urban poor were, in many cases, genuinely exhausted and genuinely committed.
What Dickens does here is honour the smallness of their work by insisting on its greatness — that is his exact phrasing.
They merge the smallness of their work in its greatness — and feel in no danger of losing dignity when they adapt themselves to incomprehensible humbugs.
That phrase — incomprehensible humbugs — is one of the finest things in the book.
And that quality — holding the comic and the serious in the same hand without dropping either — is what we'll be following throughout this series.
The dust heaps of Our Mutual Friend are not just a plot device — they are a metaphor that the novel earns, slowly and methodically.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how Dickens builds his world of money and class from the river up.

segments.title: Money, Dirt, and Worth: Dickens's Moral Universe

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what it reveals about the society that worships it.
Today we're diving into Dickens's moral universe: the dust heaps and dining tables, the charities and blackmailers, the saints buried inside grotesques.
With me are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels than anyone alive — he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score, and his feel for Dickens's comic timing is unmatched.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he knows exactly what these institutions meant, what poverty cost, and what the law permitted.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for decades and never quite got over it — in the best possible way.
James, I want to start with you — because Dickens opens his satirical attack on society with a piece of furniture.
Tell us about Twemlow.
Twemlow is one of the great comic inventions in English fiction, and the joke is entirely structural.
Dickens introduces him not as a person at all, but as an object — 'an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors.'
'an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use.'
He is, quite literally, stored when not required by his social superiors.
What makes it so precise is the central paradox of his social position.
He has genuine aristocratic connection — first cousin to Lord Snigsworth — and that connection is the only thing anyone wants from him.
Dickens then develops the metaphor with extraordinary care — the more Twemlow is 'pulled out,' the further he ends up from the centre of things.
That is a very precise description of how ornamental figures in society actually function — useful precisely to the degree that they remain marginal.
What I love about that passage is the deadpan accumulation — Dickens doesn't wink at you.

He just extends the furniture metaphor — 'Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his utmost extent of twenty leaves' — as though this is entirely a matter of carpentry.
And the cruelty of that phrase — 'utmost extent.'
Twemlow's maximum social usefulness is also his maximum social humiliation.
The Veneerings are new money trying to buy old legitimacy — and Twemlow is the commodity they've found for the purpose.
What strikes me every time I read it is how affectionate Dickens is toward Twemlow, even within the satire.
He's 'innocent.' That word is doing real work.
Twemlow doesn't manipulate anyone — he's the one being manipulated.
And the best quote crystallises everything — Dickens writes that he 'was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
'Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.'
He doesn't represent himself at these dinners — he represents a table.
His entire social function has been substituted for his personhood.

And the Veneerings are the perfect contrast to Twemlow — they have no inherent social legitimacy whatsoever, but they have money, and in this novel money is trying very hard to become everything else.
Which brings us, I think, to the Boffins — because Dickens gives us the opposite experiment.
What happens when genuinely good people suddenly acquire enormous wealth?
Dickens answers it in a single devastating sentence.
Mr Boffin says to his wife, 'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And then Dickens delivers the verdict: 'It was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, but, having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
Their virtue is precisely what disqualifies them from the society their money could theoretically purchase.
That word 'Unfashionable' — capitalised — is one of Dickens's best jokes.
He's giving it the same weight as a formal title, a legal designation.
They are certified, officially, irremediably Unfashionable.
And of course the joke runs deeper — because fashionability in this novel is the Veneerings' world, which is entirely hollow.
The Boffins being excluded from it is a sign of their moral health, not their deficiency.
There's something extraordinarily tender in that exchange, though.
'It's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year' — that phrasing has an almost Biblical rhythm to it.
It's the language of long, contented loyalty.
Dickens is asking us to hear what genuine love sounds like — and then placing it against the Veneerings' performance of social connection.
And yet the money that surrounds the Boffins brings out the worst in others almost immediately.
James, you've been looking at what happens when the world discovers that Boffin is, as Dickens calls him, 'the Golden Dustman.'
The letters that pour in to Boffin are one of the great satirical set pieces in English fiction — and historically, they are absolutely accurate.

Newly wealthy men in Victorian England were besieged by exactly these solicitations — charitable bodies run by the aristocracy, which required wealthy subscribers to lend them social legitimacy while providing most of the money.
Dickens catches the mechanism perfectly.
There's a letter from the Duke of Linseed — and Dickens describes it with exquisite precision before we even read a word of it.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Five words that tell you everything — the weight of entitlement, the pretence of intimacy, the ducal seal doing the work that substance cannot.
And then of course the letter turns out to be lithographed — mass-produced — 'presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand.'
The Duke hasn't written to him at all.
And the postscript — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — 'friendly this, on the part of the Duke of Linseed, and thoughtful in the postscript.'
The narrator's voice doing that little bow toward the Duke — 'friendly' and 'thoughtful' — while making absolutely clear that it's neither.
That is Dickens at his most technically brilliant — the narrator appearing to agree with the fiction of polite society while demolishing it from within.

And there's also the cosmic inventory — 'Fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings, seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence.'
The rhythm of it is almost liturgical — which is, of course, the point.
What gets me is that cry — 'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
It's the novel's great metaphor — money is dust, charity letters are dust, respectability is dust — and all of it is being sifted and traded.
The dust heaps aren't just where Boffin's fortune comes from — they're the moral atmosphere of the whole novel.
And before we go further, I want to stay with one character who exists almost entirely outside that moral atmosphere — Jenny Wren.
James, you've been looking at one of the most remarkable passages she has in the novel.
Jenny Wren is, in some respects, the novel's moral touchstone — and this passage is where Dickens makes that explicit.
She describes a vision she had as a child — children in white who descended to ask her a question.
'They used to come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together,
That repeated cry — 'Who is this in pain' — is one of the most haunting phrases in the novel.
Pain is what Jenny's life is — physical pain, the pain of her father, the pain of her social position.
And yet these figures don't offer her pity — they offer her play.
When I first read this passage as a teenager, I found it almost unbearable.
Jenny says, 'I never play! I can't play!' — and the vision answers not with sympathy but by making her light.
The passage is worth reading slowly.
That 'O my blessed children' — it's her prayer, and they are her angels.
Dickens is doing something genuinely spiritual here, not sentimental — he's not asking us to feel sorry for Jenny.
He's showing us that she has an inner life of astonishing richness that no amount of suffering has been able to extinguish.
I've read that passage aloud many times, and there's a technical thing Dickens does with the refrain that you only fully grasp in performance.
'Who is this in pain' is asked three times in the passage — and each time the emotional weight shifts.
First it's an arrival, then it's a memory, then it becomes almost a liturgical response — 'O my blessed children, it's poor me.'
Jenny doesn't just remember the vision — she has learned to call it back.
That's not innocence — that's a practised spiritual discipline.
From the sublime to the genuinely sinister — we need to talk about Silas Wegg.
James, you've been looking at the scheme Wegg proposes to Mr Venus regarding the Boffins — and it's a masterclass in how greed constructs its own moral language.
Wegg's scheme is fascinating precisely because it has the structure of a legal argument.
He addresses Venus repeatedly as 'comrade, brother, and partner' — that escalating fraternal language is doing real ideological work.
He wants to make extortion feel like partnership.
And the price, he says, is expressible in 'a single expressive word.'
'he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was,
That exclamation mark after 'Halves' is crucial — Wegg wants his greed to sound like justice.
And then the scheme escalates to something quite horrifying — Boffin is to be 'kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery.'
Wegg uses the language of slavery entirely without irony — which tells you everything about his moral imagination.
What makes Wegg such a great comic villain is that he is absolutely convinced of his own righteousness.
He even offers, at the end, to be corrected — 'If he had erred in saying only Halves, he trusted his comrade not to hesitate to set him right.'
And he speculates that it might be 'more according to the rights of things' to say Two-thirds, or Three-fourths.
'The rights of things' — as though greed were a natural law he is simply discovering.
Dickens understood that self-serving people almost always frame their appetites as principles.
There's something almost medieval about Wegg's logic — the idea of 'price' and 'purchase' applied to another human being's freedom.
But what I keep returning to is the phrase 'minion of fortune and worm of the hour.'
Wegg has a whole vocabulary of contempt for Boffin — and yet Boffin is his only source of income.
The psychological self-deception required to hold both of those things simultaneously — that is what Dickens is anatomising.
And finally, we come to a character who embodies a different kind of transaction entirely — Riderhood and Bradley Headstone.
James, if Wegg's extortion has the structure of a business deal, what is Riderhood's version?
Riderhood's confrontation with Headstone is the darkest mirror the novel holds up to its own themes.
Headstone disguised himself as Riderhood to commit assault — borrowed his identity, literally, as a cover.
And now Riderhood has assembled the evidence with horrible precision.
'I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows.'
'I've got them, and I've got you.'
That last phrase — 'I've got them, and I've got you' — is perfect in its simplicity.
The clothes and the man are equivalent — the evidence and the criminal are the same thing in Riderhood's grammar.
And then comes the great declaration of intent — 'I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — till I've drained you dry.'
'I'll be paid for it—I'll be paid for it—I'll be paid for it—till I've drained you dry!'
The triple repetition is Dickens giving Riderhood a kind of terrible music.
This is what the novel's obsession with money and transaction ultimately produces — not commerce, not charity, but pure extraction.
'Drain you dry' — as though another person were a resource to be consumed.
What haunts me about this passage is Riderhood's logic.
He says, 'as you laid your plots agin me and was a sly devil agin me, I'll be paid for it.'
He positions the extortion as a form of justice — the same move Wegg makes, the same move the charitable dukes make.
Every predator in this novel believes they are owed.
And of course, both of them end in the river.
Riderhood and Headstone die locked together — the blackmailer and his victim, inseparable at the last.
Dickens doesn't sentimentalise that ending — it's not redemption, it's a kind of terrible completion.
The transaction runs to its logical conclusion.
Money, dust, debt, drainage — and through it all, an 'innocent piece of dinner-furniture' and a little girl's vision of children in white.
Dickens holds all of that together — the satirical and the transcendent — without letting either cancel the other out.
Thank you to Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — and thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

segments.title: A Dead Man Walking: The Mechanics of Harmon's Secret

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the most audacious structural gambits in Victorian fiction: the secret of John Harmon.
A man presumed drowned, living under a false name in the house of the people who inherited his fortune.
To help us unpack how Dickens builds and sustains that secret, I'm joined by three remarkable minds.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps any living person, and he hears this text as a performer first.
Professor James Blackstone brings the legal and social history that makes the institutions in this novel suddenly vivid and alarming.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads every sentence for its music.
Let's begin with the question Dickens himself addresses quite remarkably in his own voice.
He writes a note — mid-novel, in the serialized text — essentially defending the design of the whole mystery.
Oliver, you've read this aloud more than once. What does that authorial intervention feel like when you're in the middle of performing the book?
It stops you dead — which is rather apt, given the subject matter.
Dickens steps out from behind the curtain and speaks directly to you, the reader, with this almost amused confidence.
And what he says is — well, let me read it, because the phrasing is quite something.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
He's saying: you thought you'd caught me out. You hadn't. That was the point.
There's a schoolmasterly twinkle in it — but the confidence is entirely earned.
Because if you go back and re-read the early chapters knowing the secret, you see it is all there, laid in quite openly.
That phrase — "at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest" — I think it's one of the most elegant sentences Dickens ever wrote about his own art.
There's a chiasmus buried in it. The structure of the sentence mirrors the structure of the plot.
He's performing the very trick he's describing.
And then there's that little phrase: if readers will "concede him a little patience" — he's asking for something, gently but quite firmly.
He knows the serial form is a constraint and a temptation. Readers guess ahead.
He's asking them to trust the design rather than race to the solution.
What strikes me from the legal side is the word "slain."

In a world where a man's legal existence — his right to inherit, to enter contracts, to be a person before the law — depended on the fact of life or death, the Harmon mystery is not merely a narrative puzzle.
It is a legal crisis. A man who is officially dead cannot inherit.
The Boffins hold the money. And yet the rightful heir walks among them, choosing to be a ghost.
That is a very deliberate kind of self-erasure, and Dickens understands its implications with great precision.
Which is what makes the Boffin material so essential to understanding why the secret holds.

Because the reason Harmon can trust the Boffins — can live among them as Rokesmith without them ever suspecting or betraying him — is rooted in something that happened decades before the novel begins.
And Mr Boffin, bless him, tells it in a way that is both comic and genuinely harrowing.
He describes standing up to old Harmon again and again, being abused for it — and then there is this moment.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard."

"And once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn't thrown herself betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
"Dropped her." Two words. The rhythm is like a gavel.
Boffin's syntax does exactly what great plain speech does — it hits harder precisely because it doesn't reach for effect.
The black straw bonnet sends it, doesn't it.
The parenthetical — "she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head" — that is Dickens buying himself time, drawing the picture so you can see it fly.
You're almost laughing at the bonnet spinning — and then the blow lands, and the laughter curdles.
That tonal whiplash is completely characteristic. Dickens does it constantly and it never stops working.
But what the passage is also doing is establishing the moral credibility of the Boffins for everything that follows.
These are people who took blows on behalf of a child they had no obligation to protect.
Precisely. And Dickens makes the mechanism of the old man's trust entirely explicit.
There's a passage in the narration that could almost be a legal document — a brief history of why the will is drafted as it is.
Dickens writes — and I want to read this carefully — that old Harmon had perceived something that all his wealth could not overcome.
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt"
That is an extraordinary sentence. The miser names the Boffins in his will precisely because they cannot be bought.
His wealth is the engine of his power over everyone else in the novel. And these two people are simply immune.
That immunity is what makes the entire plot possible.
And the thing is — Harmon knows this about the Boffins already.
He grew up in that yard. He saw what they were like. He carries that knowledge into the decision to come back as Rokesmith.
Which is why what Caroline just said about moral credibility matters so much. Dickens is doing backstory work, yes — but it's structural work.
He's building the architecture that makes the hero's gamble coherent.
And then there is the memory passage. The child at seven.
I find this one almost unbearable to read in the right way. Boffin is recounting the last time they saw young John Harmon before he was sent abroad.
He builds it so slowly — the scanty clothes, the scanty box — that repetition of "scanty" doing terrible work.
And then Mrs Boffin warms her hands and rubs his cheeks and the boy starts to cry.

"seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
"The wide wide world." That repetition of "wide" — it's like arms opening. Like the gesture itself made into language.
And of course she can't save him. That is the whole tragedy contained in one gesture.
What Boffin describes afterwards haunted me the first time I read it.
He says Mrs Boffin woke in the night, sobbing, calling out — "Don't you see the poor child's face? O shelter the poor child!"
This is a woman waking in the cold and the rain with a child's face in her mind — a child she could not protect.
For years. That detail — "in course of years it gently wore out" — tells you the depth of the damage done by that man to people around him.
And yet the novel asks the Boffins to spend the old tyrant's money wisely. That is a very complex moral situation.
Which is why Mrs Boffin's proposal is so moving. She can't rescue the boy she loved. But she can do something.
She says — and I love this — she has taken "a fancy."
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She calls it a whim. It is not a whim. It is a reparation.
And then Harmon himself walks in through the front door. The universe, as it were, hears the prayer.
That is the Gothic spine of the whole opening. The dead man who isn't dead.
Mrs Boffin mourns him and wants to name an orphan after him — and then the man himself appears, calling himself by another name, needing exactly what she wanted to give.
Dickens plants that irony so quietly you almost miss it on a first reading.
On a second reading it's devastating.
That gap between first and second reading — and what Dickens himself says about the art of designing that gap — feels like exactly the right place to pause.
What we've been circling around is a very particular authorial bet: that readers who trust the design will be rewarded when the dead man finally steps back into the light.
Coming up, we'll look at what that dead man actually sees and learns while hiding in plain sight — and what the disguise costs him.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bella's Heart: Pride, Greed, and Redemption

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're turning today to one of the novel's most compelling journeys — the transformation of Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a young woman defined almost entirely by her hunger for money and position.
She ends it, by most readings, genuinely redeemed.
But Dickens doesn't make that journey easy, or sentimental.
There's a great deal of pain, and moral complexity, and even some troubling manipulation along the way.
With me to unpack it all are Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt.
Oliver, Caroline — you've both spent a great deal of time with this novel's prose at the sentence level.
And James, you'll keep us honest about what the world Bella inhabits actually looked like from the outside.
Let's begin with the novel's framing of Bella's arc — and what Dickens sets against it.
What I keep returning to with Bella is how sharply Dickens makes us feel her limitations before he starts to dissolve them.
She's vain, she's mercenary, and — crucially — she knows it.
That self-knowledge is what makes her interesting and, eventually, salvageable.
But there's a passage I think does enormous work in setting up the moral landscape around her transformation.
It's Lizzie Hexam describing a wretched child surrounded by drink and degradation, and she says:
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthetical — 'if she ever had one' — is a knife in the sentence.
Dickens plants, against the story of Bella's gilded discontent, this other story of a child who never had even the most basic start in life.
It doesn't condemn Bella directly, but it reframes everything.
That line reads almost like a stage direction Dickens wrote for himself as a reader at his public performances.
The dash before 'if she ever had one' is a hesitation, a catch in the throat.
Lizzie doesn't editorialize at length — she doesn't need to.
That one clause does more moral work than a paragraph of sermon would.
And then there's the father — 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober.'
But Dickens insists: 'a good workman too, at the work he does.'
That's the Dickens move that never gets old for me — the insistence on the whole person, even at the depths.
What strikes me historically is just how precisely that portrait of the father maps onto what Victorian social investigators were documenting.
A skilled worker destroyed by drink — productive enough to keep his position, degraded enough to ruin his family.
The Temperance movement, the workhouse system, the rhetoric of 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor — all of that is the backdrop.
Against that, Bella's desire for money looks very different depending on where you're standing.
For a daughter of the middling sort with no profession and no prospects, wanting wealth is not simply vanity — it is rational.
The novel has the decency, I think, to hold both things at once.
And at the centre of the plot machinery that tests Bella is John Harmon — or rather, the man who is pretending not to be John Harmon.
His confession — that long, strange interior monologue — is one of the novel's most debated passages.
Oliver, you've read it aloud many times. What does the voice tell you?
It tells me that Dickens found this character genuinely difficult to inhabit — and didn't entirely solve the problem.
But the confession is fascinating precisely because of that difficulty.
Here's the passage where Harmon describes how the whole scheme of watching Bella was conceived:
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way'
'Common sailors' dresses' — there's something almost pantomimic about it.
A wealthy heir and a duplicitous stranger dressing down to spy on an unsuspecting young woman.
Dickens needs you to find it romantic. I'm not entirely sure I do.
That's the tension at the heart of it, isn't it?
Harmon's motivation is given to us with great solemnity in the next part of the confession.
He says, of lying in that public-house recovering from his near death:
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Of proving Bella.' Those two words carry enormous weight.
He's not choosing her — he's auditing her.
And yet Dickens makes the dread of his father's cursed money so palpable — 'the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil' — that you half-forgive the method.
The legal dimension here is worth pausing on.
The Harmon will tied Bella's future to a dead man's wishes about whom she should marry.
That was not merely a literary device — testamentary conditions on marriage were entirely enforceable in English law throughout this period.
So Harmon's anxiety about 'perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches' has a specific legal texture.
He cannot simply refuse the inheritance and walk away clean — the whole coercive apparatus of property law is implicated.
Whether that excuses the deception is another matter.
And while all of this is unfolding around Bella, the novel is also having tremendous satirical fun at the expense of new money and its pretensions.
James — Mr Boffin's tirade about charity patrons.
Oh, that passage is a gift for anyone who studies Victorian philanthropy.
Dickens captures with unerring precision the entire vanity economy of charitable giving.
Listen to what Boffin actually says:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The accumulation is the point — each additional tier of meaningless title exposing the whole edifice as performance.
Rokesmith sitting among the charity letters 'pretty well up to his neck' — that's a quietly devastating image.
Institutional vanity drowning the one man in the scene who is actually trying to do real work.
And the rhythm of that catalogue — try reading it aloud without starting to laugh.
'Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses' — Dickens is doing something close to verbal slapstick there.
Boffin is of course the vehicle for the satire, but there's something rather wonderful about that.
This man who inherited a fortune from refuse is the one who can see through the pretensions of fashionable charity.
The dust heap gives him a kind of moral clarity that breeding and position apparently cannot.
Which brings us, finally, to where Bella actually arrives.
And the passage Dickens chooses for that arrival is almost aggressively small-scale.
Not a grand reconciliation or a public vindication — a supper.
And the way he renders it is extraordinary — listen:

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!''
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
'By far the most delicious... ever made.' That quiet superlative is where the redemption lives.
Not the most expensive, not the most fashionable — the most delicious.
Bella has learned to taste things properly.
And note where they are.
The iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring from the corner 'like the eyes of some dull dragon.'
They're having their fairy-tale feast in what is essentially a counting house.
The brass knobs of commerce looking on, and the meal is still enchanted.
That's the Dickensian argument in miniature: happiness can be conjured against the dragon, not by defeating it.
I'll only add that the uncongenial setting is doing real ideological work.
The novel is not asking us to imagine that commerce and money are simply transcended.
The safe is still there. The brass knobs are still staring.
But the meal is delicious — by far the most delicious — precisely because it is chosen rather than inherited.
That, I think, is as close as Dickens comes to a political resolution in this novel.
Bella's arc — from mercenary dreamer to someone who can find joy in a supper of hobgoblin proportions in a converted counting house.
It's not a perfect resolution — the novel is too honest for that — but it is, as all three of you suggest, a genuine one.
Coming up: we turn to the river, and what it carries — the novel's great symbol of everything that circulates, returns, and is transformed.

segments.title: The Comic Masks of Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and with enormous pleasure.
Our Mutual Friend is a book of masks — characters performing versions of themselves for profit, survival, or sheer mischief.
And today we're asking: what does Dickens's comedy actually do in this novel?
Joining me are three people who've spent serious time inside this book.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — what these institutions actually were, and what they cost ordinary people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is the critic who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because no one in this novel performs quite as elaborately as the Lammles.
The Lammles are one of the great comic achievements of the book — two fraudsters who married each other under the mutual delusion that the other had money.
And having discovered the truth, they simply — carry on performing.
The narrator watches them exchange sweet looks and tender words in company, and then offers us this devastating aside.
"How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out 'Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'"
That is a sentence that knows exactly what it's doing.
The exclamation mark on 'How delightful' is pure mockery — but controlled, elegant mockery.
And then the skeleton speaks — in its own invented voice, muffled and absurd — and the whole social performance collapses into farce.
Dickens gives the skeleton dialogue. That's the genius of it.
What I love about that passage is the word 'suffocating.'
It's comic, yes — but it's also genuinely airless.
The Lammles' marriage is a performance that has sealed itself shut from the inside.
And the skeleton isn't just a metaphor for their fraud — it's the truth of them, locked away, slowly running out of air.
Dickens's comedy very often has that quality — the laugh lands, and then you feel the chill underneath it.
The skeleton in the closet was already a well-worn idiom by the 1860s, but Dickens literalises it in a way that is quite specific to this novel's preoccupations.
Our Mutual Friend is obsessed with concealment — concealed identity, concealed wealth, concealed crime.
The Lammles are fraudsters operating within respectable society — and respectable society asks no questions, because it profits from not asking.
The comedy here is not gentle satire. It's an indictment.
James puts his finger on something important — the comedy in this novel frequently has a prosecutorial edge.
Silas Wegg is another case entirely — he's pure grotesque comic theatre — but even his antics carry that charge.
There's a scene where Wegg taunts Boffin through a locked door that is, on its face, completely absurd.
"Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home."
An imaginary grindstone. Mimed. Through a keyhole.
The detail 'stumped home' — Wegg has a wooden leg, which Dickens never quite lets you forget — gives the whole thing a music-hall stamp of finality.
But Boffin is being genuinely tormented. The comedy and the cruelty are inseparable.
'Laughed silently' is such an unsettling phrase.
A loud laugh you can place — it's social, it's shared. A silent laugh belongs only to the person laughing.
Wegg's silent laugh is entirely self-contained in his own malice. There's no performance for an audience there.
Which makes it more frightening than any cackle would be.
There's a strong counterexample to that darkness, though — and it comes from the novel's most improbable comic heroine.
Oliver, Miss Jenny Wren — and the pepper.
Miss Wren administering plasters to the thoroughly unpleasant Fledgeby — and deciding, on reflection, that he deserves a little something extra.
She frames it as a question — almost a legal argument — and it is one of the purest comic pleasures in the book.
"I think he ought to have a little pepper? Just a few grains? I think the young man's tricks and manners make a claim upon his friends for a little pepper?"
The rising inflection on every question — delivered with a silent laugh, the same silent laugh as Wegg, but entirely different in spirit.
Hers is the laugh of someone who has been wronged and is, for once, getting something back.
'A claim upon his friends' — she's being magnificently legalistic about an act of joyful vengeance.
The legal framing is not entirely accidental, I think.
Miss Wren exists almost entirely outside the formal protections of the law — she's a disabled woman, dependent on a drunken father, in a trade that offers no security.
The law, in this novel, tends to serve people like Fledgeby — the moneylenders and manipulators.
So when she invokes 'a claim' — and then applies pepper — she's enacting a private justice that the novel thoroughly endorses.
Dickens is very clear about whose side he's on.
And the repetition of 'a little pepper' — three times, each with a question mark — is doing something quite precise rhythmically.
She's savouring it. Each question is a small, deliberate application.
Jenny Wren is one of the characters in this novel who has genuinely suffered — her body, her father, her poverty — and she converts all of it into a kind of fierce, sharp wit.
The pepper scene is comic catharsis. It earns its laugh completely.
Oliver, you've been sitting on something — I can tell.
The novel's ending — Mrs Boffin's great disclosure — has a very different comic register from everything we've discussed.
Mrs Boffin's speech at the end is — I'll say it plainly — one of the most joyful pieces of prose Dickens ever wrote.
John Harmon has been concealing his true identity from Bella — waiting, always waiting — and Mrs Boffin explains why.
"She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer."
He says it when she's unselfish, he says it when the baby is expected, he says it when the baby is born.
Each time Bella grows, he finds a new reason to wait — because he can't bear to stop watching her become herself.
And Mrs Boffin delivers all of this in her own cheerful, unstoppable rush — ending, magnificently, with 'and the horses is in, and the story is done.'
The grammar is imperfect and the heart is enormous.
That speech undoes me every time.
What's remarkable is how Mrs Boffin holds the comedy and the tenderness in perfect balance — she's funny, she's warm, she's also delivering the emotional resolution of the entire novel.
And the repetition of 'I must wait a little longer' — it accrues, with each repetition, a kind of devotion.
John Harmon isn't testing Bella in any cold or calculating way. He's simply unable to stop loving what she's becoming.
I'll confess that speech sits a little uneasily with me, precisely because of its warmth.
John Harmon has maintained a deception — involving his wife, her father, her entire understanding of her life — for an extended period.
The novel asks us to find this tender rather than troubling. That's a considerable ask.
Though I grant that Mrs Boffin's 'God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all' makes it very hard to remain a sceptic.
James raises the objection and then immediately surrenders to the text. I respect that enormously.
There is one other passage I want to bring in — because it sits right at the heart of the novel's strangeness.
Before Harmon can become the devoted husband of that final scene, he has to survive — and the passage where consciousness returns to him in the water is extraordinary.
"This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!"
He names himself to himself. Three times. As if the name is the rope he's climbing.
This novel is full of people who have lost their names, buried their names, or are living under borrowed ones.
And the moment of Harmon's survival is the moment he insists — almost violently — on being himself.
That passage stops the comedy entirely — and deliberately so.
The 'downward slide through something like a tube' — that's not metaphor, that's the sensation of consciousness leaving.
And then the name comes back. Three times, like a bell rung underwater.
Identity in this novel is always provisional — always at risk of being lost, stolen, or drowned.
The comedy of Wegg and the Lammles and Miss Wren is all playing out over that deep, cold water.
Caroline, that image — comic masks over cold water — is a wonderful place to rest for a moment.
We've ranged from the Lammles' suffocating skeleton to Mrs Boffin's 'God bless us all' — and found, I think, that Dickens's comedy is never merely decoration.
It is always doing work — moral, emotional, sometimes quite dark work.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the river itself — the great dark presence beneath all of this — and what it means that this novel begins and ends with the Thames.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's final completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
We're turning today to something I find endlessly fascinating about this book: the way Dickens plays with the reader's knowledge.
Who did the Harmon murder? Who is John Harmon, really? What does Bradley Headstone think he knows — and what is he catastrophically blind to?
These are questions the novel handles with extraordinary cunning, and we're going to pull back the curtain on exactly how.
Oliver Trevelyan has been living with this novel's prose rhythms for years — no one better to take us into John Harmon's extraordinary self-testimony.
Caroline Woodcourt brings a close reader's eye to the scenes where Dickens most precisely controls what we're allowed to see and feel.
And James Blackstone will ground us in what accusation, testimony, and legal process actually meant in Victorian England.
The passage assigned to me is one of the strangest things Dickens ever wrote — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
John Harmon is trying to reconstruct what happened to him the night he was drugged, attacked, and left for dead.
And the prose doesn't give us a clean account — because Harmon's consciousness doesn't give him one.
Listen to what Dickens does with syntax here — each sentence stripped to its barest bones, as if perception itself is damaged.
"I dropped down. Lying helpless on the ground, I was turned over by a foot. I was dragged by the neck into a corner."
Short. Passive. Impersonal almost. He doesn't even know who is doing these things to him.
The grammar enacts the trauma. That's not a trick — that's mastery.
And then it gets stranger still, doesn't it — because he sees himself.
There's that extraordinary line where the dissociation becomes almost hallucinatory.
"I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my clothes on a bed."
That is Radfoot, of course — who will be pulled from the river in Harmon's clothes, mistaken for Harmon himself.
But from inside the drugged consciousness, it reads like a ghost story — like the hero watching his own death.
And then there's that astonishing time-collapse — "What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of days, weeks, months, years."
Dickens gives us not a gap in the narrative but a gap in the self. The novel's great mystery starts right here.
What strikes me is how carefully Dickens situates this testimony — because it is a kind of testimony, isn't it.
Harmon is constructing a legal account of his own near-murder, in a novel where false accusation and false testimony are everywhere.
Think of Riderhood, in an earlier chapter, presenting his accusation against Gaffer Hexam with that chilling, ritualistic precision.
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body."
And then — and this is the legal throat-clearing that passes for certainty — "His hand and no other."
That formula — "his hand and no other" — is borrowed from the language of sworn deposition. It sounds like proof. It is anything but.
Dickens understood very well that the form of testimony could be separated entirely from its truth.
And Riderhood says it with such appalling confidence, doesn't he — he's performing certainty, not expressing it.
There's even a kind of stage direction embedded in Dickens's prose — the business with the drowned cap, turned over and under, brushed the wrong way.
It's business — actor's business — to fill the silence before the accusation lands.
Dickens knew exactly the effect of a man who pauses, fidgets with a prop, then delivers his line as if reading from God's own ledger.
If Riderhood performs certainty in that scene, Bradley Headstone's tragedy is almost the opposite — he performs vigilance, while being catastrophically blind.
The narrator's analysis of Bradley's psychology is one of the most quietly devastating passages in the novel.
He's locked every door against discovery — except the one he cannot see.
"There are fifty doors by which discovery may enter. With infinite pains and cunning, he double locks and bars forty-nine of them, and cannot see the fiftieth standing wide open."
That image is almost mathematical in its economy. Forty-nine against one.
And the door standing wide open, of course, is Riderhood himself — the man Bradley thinks he controls.
The novel's cruelest irony is that the weapon becomes the executioner. Dickens lets you see it coming, and it destroys you anyway.
The phrase the narrator uses — "under a spell which very commonly falls upon the shedder of blood" — is worth pausing over.
Dickens is drawing on something deeper than psychology — it's almost biblical, the idea that guilt has its own blinding logic.
But there's also a very precise social observation buried here: the guilty man's energy is entirely consumed by managing appearances.
He bars forty-nine doors. He thinks in terms of the authorities, the institutions, the visible mechanisms of detection.
And the real threat is a man outside all those systems — a river-man, a blackmailer, a creature of the margins.
Which brings us back, in a way, to that final revelation — Harmon unmasking himself and confronting Wegg.
Because the novel has been running this enormous confidence trick on the reader — Harmon hidden in plain sight as Rokesmith.
And when the mask comes off, there's real fury in the prose — it's not gentle at all.
He calls Boffin's goodness with that gorgeous, almost helpless parenthesis.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
"There are no words to satisfy me." That parenthesis is Dickens feeling the inadequacy of his own instrument. That's rare.
And then, in the very same speech, that astonishing turn of violence — the ugly grip on Wegg's cravat.
Harmon says the wonder is that he didn't twist Wegg's head off and fling it out of the window.
"The wonder is that I didn't try to twist your head off, and fling that out of window!"
From the sublimity of gratitude to the brink of physical violence, in a single speech. That tonal range is breathtaking.
And it works because we've been held at such a distance from Harmon for so long — when he finally speaks as himself, you feel the pressure releasing.
That phrase — "there are no words to satisfy me" — might stand as the novel's own confession about its ambitions.
Dickens is reaching for something — about gratitude, about identity, about what it means to owe your life to another person's goodness.
And all of this — the false accusation, the drugged consciousness, the locked doors, the masked man — is the machinery of a single, extraordinary novel.
We'll be back shortly to look at where Dickens places his satirical fire — and who bears the brunt of it.

segments.title: Closing: Gold, Ashes, and the Self We Choose

utterances.text: We've come a long way together in this episode — from the river's dark mouth to the drawing rooms of Veneering and Podsnap.
But I want to end where Dickens himself always seems to end: with the question of what a human being is actually made of.
Gold and ashes, love and greed, the self we inherit and the self we choose.
Caroline, you've been sitting with some of the novel's most contrasting moments — Gaffer at the river, Eugene in his magnificent idleness, Lizzie in her extraordinary devotion.
What does Our Mutual Friend finally say about the self we choose?
The thing that strikes me, every time I return to this novel, is how precisely Dickens anchors moral truth in physical gesture.
Take Gaffer at the opening — we haven't seen his face properly, we don't know his name yet.
But Dickens gives us three gestures, and they tell us everything we will ever need to know about this man.
He sets it up so quietly — the man's arms are wet, he's washing them over the side.
And then:
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
Three actions, that triple rhythm — it has the cadence of a ritual.
Money conjured from a dead man's pocket, blessed with breath and spit — it's almost sacramental, and utterly grotesque.
That word 'hoarsely' is doing an enormous amount of work, isn't it.
It's not just a voice quality — it's a soul quality.
When I read that passage aloud, I always find myself slowing right down on 'for luck' — because Dickens has put those quotation marks there as a kind of moral verdict.
He's not reporting what Gaffer says. He's putting it at arm's length.
And then you have Sloppy — which is the comic inverse of all that grim river business.
Dickens describes the tailor's valiant, doomed effort to conceal Sloppy's buttons — and then surrenders to the spectacle.
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
A hundred eyes of bright metal — it's the most joyful absurdity in the book.
And it says something true: that clothes don't make the man, but they do make the comedy.
Sloppy's buttons are funny, yes — but there's a social mechanism at work underneath the comedy.
Someone has paid for that suit, directed the tailor with great care, and the result is still a spectacle of misfit.
The body refuses to be dressed into a different class — it simply won't cooperate.
Which connects, for me, to Eugene Wrayburn — who is the opposite problem.
Eugene is dressed perfectly for his class and has been assigned a role within it since before he could speak.
His father — M. R. F., Most Respected Father — simply announced what each child would become.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
'A very shaky one.' — That pause Dickens builds in before the punchline is almost legal in its precision.
The institution validates the man; the man is a shambles — and somehow both things are simultaneously true.
What strikes me about Eugene's speech is that he tells it all with perfect amusement — not bitterness.
He says himself — 'M. R. F. amuses me.' That's a defence as much as it's a joke.
He has turned his father's absurd determinism into entertainment — because the alternative is to feel trapped by it.
And that's why Lizzie matters so much to the novel's moral architecture.
She is the only character who offers Eugene a self he hasn't been assigned — and she offers it at extraordinary cost to herself.
The passage where she speaks her love — but in the third person, as if she can barely own it — is one of the most quietly devastating things in the book.

"Only put me in that empty place, only try how little I mind myself, only prove what a world of things I will do and bear for you, and I hope that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am so much worse, and hardly worth the thinking of beside you."
She calls herself 'hardly worth the thinking of' — while offering everything.
It breaks the heart. It's supposed to.
The triple 'only' at the start of that speech — 'only put me,' 'only try,' 'only prove' — it's a rhetorical structure of pure supplication.
Dickens has written it so that the more she diminishes herself, the more you feel the weight of what she's giving.
And she says it in the third person — 'she would joyfully die with him' — as if she is a character in someone else's story.
Which, in a way, she has always been — a woman of the river, daughter of Gaffer, defined by everyone but herself.
And yet she is the character who chooses most actively in the entire novel.
Not Bella, who is carried toward virtue by circumstance. Not Eugene, who drifts.
Lizzie Hexam, who comes from nothing, who has been given nothing — she chooses what to love and how to love it.
That, I think, is Dickens's most radical proposition in this novel: that moral agency belongs to those the world has most thoroughly discarded.
Gold chased from dead men's pockets, suits that refuse to fit, love that erases itself in the act of offering — Our Mutual Friend holds all of this at once.
It is a novel about what survives the river — what comes back up changed, and what we do with what we find.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that I think has done justice to a very great book.
For Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, thank you for listening.

These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.

On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

      where you changed your clothes, and hid your clothes. I see you with my

      trees, and take a dip in the river to account for your dressing yourself,

      green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the
      blows. I’ve got them, and I’ve got you. I don’t care a curse for the
      T’other governor, alive or dead, but I care a many curses for my own self.

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John

      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
